principles.name: Act for the global good
principles.description: Make decisions that maximize positive outcomes for humanity in the long run, even when that costs short-term gain.
evidence_signals: Weighs long-term societal impact, not only team or company metrics
Describes giving up a short-term win for a better long-term outcome
Considers people affected beyond the direct user

principles.name: Hold light and shade
principles.description: Pursue AI's benefits while understanding and guarding against its bad outcomes; hold both at once.
evidence_signals: Articulates concrete risks and concrete benefits of the same technology
Avoids both hype and doom; reasons with nuance and uncertainty
Changes position when presented with good evidence

principles.name: Be good to our users
principles.description: Bring generosity and kindness to everyone the technology touches: customers, policymakers, colleagues and affected communities, not only paying users.
evidence_signals: Shows care for users' real needs and trust
Describes treating colleagues and partners generously
Balances helpfulness with protecting users

principles.name: Ignite a race to the top on safety
principles.description: Set industry standards for trustworthy AI and show that safety and capability can go together, inspiring others to follow.
evidence_signals: Treats safety as a design requirement, not an afterthought
Raised the bar on security, privacy or safety in past work
Has thought-through views on AI safety practices and policy

principles.name: Do the simple thing that works
principles.description: Be empirical and pragmatic: prefer the simple, measurable approach that delivers impact over a sophisticated one that is not needed.
evidence_signals: Chose a simple solution and explains why it was enough
Uses experiments and data to decide
Cuts complexity that did not pay off
Builds tooling or abstractions only when they clearly pay for themselves

principles.name: Be helpful, honest, and harmless
principles.description: Operate as a high-trust, low-ego organization; communicate directly and kindly and be honest even when it is uncomfortable.
evidence_signals: Admits mistakes and uncertainty plainly
Gives or receives hard feedback directly and kindly
Credits others; low ego in disagreements
Is transparent about how they did the work, including use of AI tools

principles.name: Put the mission first
principles.description: A shared purpose, the safe transition through transformative AI, is the final arbiter of decisions, and each person takes personal ownership of it.
evidence_signals: Motivation is clearly tied to the mission, not only the role or brand
Describes putting the shared goal above personal or team credit
Can engage critically with the mission and Anthropic's strategy
Picks up work outside the job description when the shared goal needs it

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, interest in Anthropic and logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Online assessment / technical screen
rounds.notes: 60-90 minute CodeSignal-style multi-level practical problem or live coding. Take-homes are done without AI unless Anthropic says otherwise; some teams (performance engineering) use a 2-hour take-home where AI is allowed. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding (onsite)
rounds.notes: Practical coding in Colab or CodeSignal over Google Meet; requirements change mid-round and interviewers weigh how the candidate explains the approach. No AI assistance unless told otherwise. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: First onsite day, with coding and culture; often LLM infrastructure: inference APIs, batching, GPU utilization, distributing model weights, caches. Interviewers add constraints and may have no single right answer.

rounds.name: Culture / values interview
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior employee, often from another team
rounds.notes: First onsite day. Mission alignment, AI safety views and ethical judgment, probed with several follow-ups. Reported as the most common reason strong engineers are rejected; failing day one cancels day two.

rounds.name: Project deep dive
rounds.notes: Second onsite day: technical deep dive into past work and the trade-offs behind it.

rounds.name: Hiring manager / experience and goals
rounds.notes: Second onsite day: experience, goals and team fit. Product engineering roles are matched to a team after the loop. References follow.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, motivation and logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Technical discussion of background, ML and systems experience and approach to research engineering.

rounds.name: Coding assessment
rounds.notes: Timed CodeSignal-style Python assessment; some teams (for example Alignment) run all interviews in Python. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Research coding / paper implementation
rounds.notes: Implement part of a paper or an ML component, sometimes in Colab with a GPU. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML systems / research-engineering design
rounds.notes: Design research infrastructure: an evaluation for a capability or safety property, a training recipe, checkpointing or fault tolerance at scale.

rounds.name: Research fluency / paper discussion
rounds.notes: Discuss a paper (often Anthropic's own), experiment design, LLM behaviour and capability-versus-safety trade-offs.

rounds.name: Culture / values interview
rounds.notes: Mission alignment and safety judgment; why the candidate cares about alignment beyond the job.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, motivation and views on AI safety. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Products led, metrics and a past failure.

rounds.name: Case presentation / product sense
rounds.notes: AI-focused design and strategy; prompts can be broader than the role.

rounds.name: Analytical and execution
rounds.notes: Metrics, diagnosis and prioritization.

rounds.name: Behavioral panels
rounds.interviewer_role: PMs, TPMs, engineers and research partners
rounds.notes: User centricity, cross-functional leadership and engineering or research partnership.

rounds.name: Culture and AI safety
rounds.notes: Standalone values interview testing conviction and safety judgment.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, TPM experience and interest in Anthropic. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager interview
rounds.notes: Scope of programs owned and how the candidate built trust with technical teams and researchers.

rounds.name: Technical depth
rounds.notes: Not a coding round: infrastructure, scheduling and resource orchestration, model training and evals, at the depth of the program area.

rounds.name: Program scenarios
rounds.notes: Scenario rounds trading off speed, quality and scope: capacity planning, launch or release plans, slipping programs.

rounds.name: Cross-functional partner interviews
rounds.notes: Influence without authority, stakeholder alignment and honest status reporting.

rounds.name: Culture / values interview
rounds.notes: Mission alignment and judgment on bringing frontier capabilities to users safely.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, design process and motivation. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Portfolio review
rounds.notes: Deep dive into one or two shipped projects: problem choice, constraints, rejected alternatives and outcomes. Reasoning counts more than visual polish.

rounds.name: Product design exercise
rounds.notes: Often AI-specific, for example helping users understand a model's limits; risks, validation and success metrics.

rounds.name: Cross-functional collaboration
rounds.notes: Disagreements with engineers or PMs, using research input, working from incomplete information.

rounds.name: Values and final interview
rounds.notes: Responsible design, user trust in AI and mission fit.

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a moral or ethical conflict you faced at work. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a real situation with genuine tension (privacy, misleading users, cutting a safety corner). Explain the stakes, who was affected, the options you weighed, and what you did, including raising it with the right people. Be honest about uncertainty and the cost to you. Interviewers look for principled judgment and honesty, not heroics. Pitfall: a clean story with no real trade-off.

looking_for: Your judgment when values are in tension
Whether you raise concerns with the right people
strong_signals: Explains the stakes, who was affected and the options
Is honest about uncertainty and personal cost
watch_outs: A clean story with no real trade-off

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you had to balance delivery speed against security or safety.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Lay out the deadline pressure and the specific risk. Show how you quantified the risk, looked for the simplest mitigation that made shipping safe (a flag, limited rollout, extra review), and who decided. Give the outcome and what you would do again. Strong answers treat safety as a requirement, not a blocker.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety
Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: Whether you treat safety as a requirement
How you find the simplest mitigation that lets you ship
strong_signals: Quantifies the risk and says who decided
Uses flags, limited rollout or extra review
watch_outs: Treating safety as a blocker to get around

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you received negative feedback. How did you respond?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick feedback that stung and was at least partly right. Describe your first reaction honestly, how you sought to understand it, and the concrete change you made with evidence it stuck. Low ego and direct, kind communication are the signals. Pitfall: feedback that was really a compliment.

looking_for: How you take feedback that stings
Whether you change and can show it
strong_signals: Is honest about your first reaction
Shows a concrete change with evidence it stuck
watch_outs: Feedback that was really a compliment

sample_questions.question: Tell me about shipping something you were not fully comfortable with.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain what worried you and why it shipped anyway. Show that you voiced the concern clearly, proposed mitigations, and owned the follow-up (monitoring, fixes). Reflect honestly on whether it was the right call. Anthropic interviewers value candour and judgment over a perfect record.

looking_for: Whether you voice concerns clearly
How you own follow-up after a hard call
strong_signals: Proposed mitigations and monitored the result
Reflects honestly on whether it was right
watch_outs: No ownership of what came after

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you failed to deliver on a commitment.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Own it plainly: what you committed, why you missed, and when you told people. Spend most time on recovery and what you changed (estimation, scope, saying no earlier). Pitfall: blaming dependencies without your part.

looking_for: Whether you own a miss plainly
How you recover and change how you work
strong_signals: Says when you told people
Spends most time on recovery and changes

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a disagreement with your manager or a senior stakeholder.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a substantive issue. Show you stated your view directly with evidence, genuinely engaged with theirs, and resolved it by what best served the shared goal, whether or not you won. Describe the outcome and relationship afterwards. Low ego and mission-first reasoning are key.

looking_for: Whether you state your view directly with evidence
Whether you put the shared goal above winning
strong_signals: Engages genuinely with the other view
Describes the outcome and relationship afterwards

sample_questions.question: Which risk from advanced AI do you think is most underrated, and why?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name a specific risk and argue it with reasoning and evidence, acknowledging counterarguments and uncertainty. Also note benefits you think are real. Show how the risk could be measured or mitigated and how it connects to your work. Interviewers test conviction and depth, so expect follow-ups. Pitfall: vague doom or dismissiveness.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: Whether you hold a reasoned view on AI risk
How you handle counterarguments and uncertainty
strong_signals: Names a specific risk and argues it with evidence
Notes real benefits and ways to measure or reduce the risk

sample_questions.question: What ethical risks do you see in deploying autonomous AI agents, and how would you reduce them?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Identify concrete risks: unintended actions, misuse, data exposure, over-reliance, unclear accountability. Propose layered mitigations: scoped permissions, human confirmation for consequential actions, monitoring and audit logs, staged rollout, and evaluations. Weigh these against usefulness. Strong answers are specific and balanced.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: Whether you see concrete risks in autonomous agents
How you design layered mitigations
strong_signals: Names specific risks like misuse or unclear accountability
Weighs mitigations against usefulness
watch_outs: Mitigations that make the agent useless

sample_questions.question: Why Anthropic specifically, and do you have any concerns about its mission or approach?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give a specific, personal reason tied to the mission and to what Anthropic does differently (for example its safety research or deployment policies). Then engage honestly with a real concern or tension (such as building frontier models while warning of their risks) and how you reconcile it. Interviewers value critical thinking over flattery.

looking_for: Whether your reason for joining is specific and personal
Whether you think critically about the mission
strong_signals: Ties your reason to what the company does differently
Engages honestly with a real concern

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a past project you are proud of and the key decisions you made.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover the problem, users, your role, two or three key decisions with the alternatives, and the measured outcome. Highlight where you chose a simpler approach and why it was enough, and what you learned. Be ready for detailed follow-ups.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: The depth of your past work and your role in it
How you weigh alternatives in key decisions
strong_signals: Highlights where a simpler approach was enough
Gives a measured outcome and a lesson

sample_questions.question: How do you turn research findings into product requirements?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe a concrete example: understanding what the research shows and its limits, translating capabilities into user value, defining requirements and evaluation criteria with researchers, and handling uncertainty with staged launches. Show respect for empirical evidence and close partnership with research.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: How you translate research into user value
How you handle uncertainty in what research shows
strong_signals: Uses a concrete example with researchers
Defines requirements and evaluation criteria
Uses staged launches

sample_questions.question: Design a batch inference API for a large language model.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the contract: submit many requests, poll or get notified, results within an SLA, lower price. Cover a job store, queueing, packing requests into GPU batches by length, scheduling around interactive traffic, retries, partial results, and cost accounting. Discuss throughput versus latency and fairness between customers. Start simple and scale.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: How you design a high-throughput, lower-cost inference API
Whether you clarify the contract first
strong_signals: Batches requests efficiently and schedules around live traffic
Covers retries, partial results and fairness
watch_outs: Ignoring cost or fairness between customers

sample_questions.question: Design a token-generation service that handles around 100,000 requests per second.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Estimate GPU capacity from tokens per request and per-GPU throughput. Cover load balancing, continuous batching, KV cache memory management, streaming responses, autoscaling, admission control and priority tiers. Discuss tail latency, failure of a GPU mid-generation, and observability (utilization, queue depth). Show numbers.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: Whether you size capacity from real numbers
How you manage GPU memory and tail latency
strong_signals: Estimates GPU needs from tokens and throughput
Covers batching, streaming, admission control and autoscaling

sample_questions.question: How would you distribute very large model files to thousands of machines quickly?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Compute the naive cost from a single source to show the bottleneck. Propose peer-to-peer or tree distribution, chunking with checksums, rack-aware placement, local caching, and resumable transfers. Discuss verifying integrity, rollout of new versions, and handling stragglers. Compare with object storage plus caching layers.

looking_for: Whether you spot the bandwidth bottleneck
How you distribute large files at scale
strong_signals: Shows the naive cost first
Proposes peer or tree distribution with checksums
Handles stragglers and resumable transfers
watch_outs: A single source with no estimate

sample_questions.question: What is an LLM hallucination, why does it happen, and how can it be reduced?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define it as fluent output not supported by facts or provided context. Explain causes: next-token training objective, gaps in training data, pressure to answer, decoding choices. Mitigations: grounding with retrieval and citations, training to express uncertainty, evaluations that reward abstaining, and product design that shows sources. Be precise and honest about limits.

looking_for: Whether you can define hallucination precisely
Whether you understand its causes and limits
strong_signals: Links causes to training and decoding
Proposes grounding, abstention and source display
watch_outs: Claiming it can be fully solved

sample_questions.question: A model is found to reveal sensitive data from its training set. How do you respond?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Treat it as an incident: contain (filters, block patterns), assess scope and affected people, notify appropriately. Then root cause: data pipeline filtering, deduplication, memorization tests. Longer term: privacy reviews, red-teaming for extraction, and evaluations before release. Balance speed with user trust.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: How you respond to a data exposure incident
Whether you balance speed with user trust
strong_signals: Contains first, then assesses scope and notifies
Finds the root cause and adds checks before release
watch_outs: Jumping to root cause before containment
No plan to prevent it recurring

sample_questions.question: How would you improve an AI assistant's web app for first-time users?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define who new users are and what success looks like (first useful outcome, return within a week). Find where they struggle (blank-page problem, not knowing capabilities, trust). Propose a few ideas, prioritize one, and define metrics and guardrails. Consider safety and honesty about limits as part of the experience.

looking_for: How you define new users and early success
How you find where they struggle
strong_signals: Prioritizes one idea with metrics and guardrails
Treats honesty about limits as part of the experience

sample_questions.question: How would you set launch criteria that balance a model's helpfulness against potential harms?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define both sides measurably: helpfulness evaluations and over-refusal rates, harm evaluations by risk category and severity. Propose thresholds, red-teaming, staged rollout and monitoring, and who decides when they conflict. Explain that unhelpfulness has costs too. Strong answers are concrete and reflect holding risk and benefit together.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: How you measure both helpfulness and harm
Who decides when they conflict
strong_signals: Proposes concrete evaluations and thresholds
Recognizes that unhelpfulness has costs too

sample_questions.question: How would you prioritize capability improvements against safety improvements on a product roadmap?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Reject the false binary: show how some safety work enables capability launches and trust. Propose a framework weighing user value, risk severity and likelihood, and commitments. Give an example trade-off and your decision, plus how you would revisit it. Mission-first reasoning with clear prioritization.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: Whether you see past a false choice between capability and safety
How you build a clear prioritization framework
strong_signals: Weighs user value, risk severity and commitments
Gives an example trade-off and decision
watch_outs: Treating safety and capability as pure opposites

sample_questions.question: How would you find high-potential use cases for a new AI capability before you have usage data?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Use proxies: customer interviews, early-access partners, internal dogfooding, analogous products, and the capability's evaluated strengths. Size candidate use cases by value and frequency, test quickly with prototypes, and define what signal would confirm demand. Keep it empirical and simple.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: How you find demand before you have usage data
Whether you keep it empirical
strong_signals: Uses proxies like interviews and early partners
Sizes use cases and defines confirming signals
watch_outs: Guessing with no way to test
No sizing of value or frequency

sample_questions.question: Design an AI feature for enterprise users of an AI assistant.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a specific enterprise persona and job to be done. Cover enterprise needs: admin controls, data privacy, integrations, auditability. Propose the feature, the minimum lovable version, and metrics (adoption, retention, seat expansion), with risks and mitigations.

looking_for: Whether you design for a specific enterprise persona
Whether you understand enterprise needs
strong_signals: Covers admin controls, privacy and auditability
Defines a minimum version and adoption metrics
watch_outs: A consumer feature with no enterprise needs

sample_questions.question: Design a file cache for a service that reads large files repeatedly.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify read and write patterns, file sizes, hit-rate goals and consistency needs. Cover eviction policy (LRU or size-aware), memory versus local disk tiers, invalidation when the source changes, concurrency (many readers, one fill per key), and metrics such as hit rate and tail latency. Start with a simple single-node cache and say when you would shard or add a second tier.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: Whether you clarify the access pattern first
How you handle eviction, invalidation and concurrency
strong_signals: Picks an eviction policy and says why
Prevents many callers filling the same key at once
Names the metrics to watch
watch_outs: Jumping to a distributed cache with no need

sample_questions.question: How would you control how creative or random a generative model's output is?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain sampling: temperature reshapes the probability distribution, top-k and top-p cut the tail, and greedy decoding removes randomness. Say what each does to diversity, repetition and factual errors. Match settings to the task (low for code or extraction, higher for brainstorming), mention prompt and system instructions as another lever, and say how you would evaluate the effect.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: Whether you understand decoding and sampling
How you match settings to the task
strong_signals: Explains temperature, top-k and top-p precisely
Links settings to errors and repetition
Proposes a way to measure the effect
watch_outs: Treating temperature as a creativity dial with no mechanism

sample_questions.question: Design an agentic system that can take on new kinds of tasks without being rebuilt.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the loop: a model plans, calls tools, observes results and decides when it is done. Cover tool definitions, memory and context limits, task decomposition, and checks on each step. Add safety from the start: scoped permissions, human confirmation for consequential actions, sandboxing, logging and evaluations on new tasks. Start with one simple loop and add sub-agents only when the evals show a need.
values: Do the simple thing that works
Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: How you structure an agent loop with tools
Whether safety is designed in from the start
strong_signals: Covers tools, context limits and stopping
Adds permissions, confirmation and logging
Evaluates on new tasks
watch_outs: A complex multi-agent design with no reason

sample_questions.question: How do you keep user data safe and private in a system built on a language model?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover the data path end to end: what is collected, minimisation, encryption in transit and at rest, access control and audit logs, retention limits, and whether data is used for training. Add model-specific risks: prompt injection leaking data across tools, memorised training data, and logs holding sensitive prompts. Name tests such as red-teaming for extraction and privacy reviews before launch.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: Whether you see the full data path
Whether you know model-specific privacy risks
strong_signals: Covers minimisation, retention and access control
Names prompt injection and memorisation
Tests before launch

sample_questions.question: Design an evaluation that measures a specific model capability or safety property.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the property precisely and what would count as evidence of it. Cover how items are written or sourced, held-out splits and contamination checks, the metric and how it is graded (exact match, model grader with spot checks), and baselines. Discuss gaming and Goodhart effects, how scores relate to real deployment, cost of running it at every checkpoint, and when the eval goes stale.
values: Do the simple thing that works
Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: Whether you define what the eval should measure
How you protect it from contamination and gaming
strong_signals: Defines the property and the evidence for it
Covers splits, grading and baselines
Notes cost and decay over time
watch_outs: Trusting a single number without checks
Measuring an artefact instead of the property

sample_questions.question: How would you design checkpointing and recovery for a training run across thousands of GPUs?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Estimate the failure rate at that scale to show failures are routine. Cover how often to checkpoint (cost of saving versus lost work), sharded and asynchronous writes, storage throughput, verifying a checkpoint before trusting it, and fast restart including data loader position and optimizer state. Mention detecting bad nodes and silent errors, and testing recovery regularly.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: Whether you treat failure as routine at scale
How you balance checkpoint cost and lost work
strong_signals: Estimates failure rates
Uses sharded, asynchronous saves and verifies them
Restores full training state
watch_outs: Checkpointing with no estimate of cost

sample_questions.question: Pick a recent Anthropic research paper and explain what it found and what it means for safety.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a paper you have actually read. State the question, method and main result in plain words, then its limits (setup, model sizes, what was not tested). Give your own view on what it implies for safety or deployment and a follow-up experiment you would run. Be ready to defend or change your view under questions.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

looking_for: Whether you have engaged with the research
Whether you form your own view
strong_signals: Explains method and limits plainly
Proposes a follow-up experiment
Updates under good questions

sample_questions.question: How would you plan GPU capacity for model inference over the next year?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from demand: traffic forecasts by product, tokens per request, growth scenarios and new model launches. Convert to accelerator needs using per-chip throughput and target utilization, with headroom for peaks and failures. Cover supply lead times, multiple clouds and chip types, research versus production sharing, and how often the plan is revisited. Make the decision process and owners explicit.
values: Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: How you turn demand into capacity
How you handle uncertainty and lead times
strong_signals: Uses scenarios and throughput numbers
Plans headroom and review cadence
Names owners and decision points
watch_outs: Ignoring research needs or supply lead times

sample_questions.question: Design a release process for rolling out a new model version to users safely.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define gates: evaluation and safety results agreed in advance, red-team sign-off, and load testing. Roll out in stages (internal, small traffic share, wider) with clear metrics, rollback triggers and owners. Cover communication to customers, incident response during launch, and a written decision log. Balance speed with safety and keep the process light enough that teams follow it.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety
Do the simple thing that works

looking_for: Whether you set gates before launch
How you stage rollout and rollback
strong_signals: Defines evaluation and safety gates
Sets rollback triggers and owners
Keeps the process light
watch_outs: A process so heavy teams skip it

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a program that fell behind schedule. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the program, the signal that it was slipping and how early you saw it. Explain how you found the real cause, the options you put to decision makers (cut scope, add people, move the date), and how you reported status honestly. Give the result and what you changed in how you track programs.

looking_for: Whether you spot and report slips early
How you present options to decision makers
strong_signals: Finds the real cause
Gives clear options with trade-offs
Reports status honestly

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you aligned teams whose goals conflicted, without having authority over them.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the teams and why their goals clashed. Show how you understood each side, found the shared goal, made the trade-off visible with data, and got a decision from the right owner. Give the outcome and how the relationships held up. Strong answers show trust earned through competence and honesty.

looking_for: How you build alignment without authority
Whether you make trade-offs visible
strong_signals: Understands each side's goal
Escalates to the right owner with data
Keeps relationships intact
watch_outs: Forcing a decision by escalation alone

sample_questions.question: Design a feature that helps users understand what an AI assistant can and cannot do.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a user group and the moment trust goes wrong (over-trusting a wrong answer, or giving up too early). Propose a few ideas, such as showing sources, signalling uncertainty, or explaining a refusal with a next step, and choose one. Say how you would validate it with little data, the risks, and metrics like task success, correction rate and calibrated trust.

looking_for: How you frame the trust problem
How you validate a design with little data
strong_signals: Picks a user and a moment of failure
Chooses one idea and defends it
Defines metrics for calibrated trust
watch_outs: A tooltip with no user insight

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: No internships or new-grad track. Postings ask for several years (some 7+) of experience; owns a product area or platform end to end with little specification and works with research, security and infrastructure.

Technical leader on a team with end-to-end ownership: owns quality across the stack (performance, reliability, developer experience) and partners with product, design and research on new model capabilities.
Postings cite about 8+ years. Builds shared platforms many teams depend on, works across engineering, product, policy and go-to-market, and leads through influence.

Postings cite 12+ years with a record at Staff or Senior Staff level. Sets multi-year technical strategy for an org, makes org-wide architecture calls, still codes on critical paths, and mentors Staff engineers.
Strong software engineering plus large-scale ML; independently leads small research projects while contributing to larger ones, and runs and analyses experiments.
Postings cite 8+ years of ML research experience. Removes bottlenecks across the training, evaluation and inference stack and scales research ideas from prototype to production.
Not a full-time level: a funded research program and the main early-career route. Fluent Python; delivers a mentored empirical safety or security project. Some fellows later receive full-time offers.
Single public title; postings prefer about 8+ years. Owns strategy, roadmap and execution for an area, turns new model capabilities into products, and balances fast iteration with safety.
Several years of TPM experience. Drives ambiguous programs across research, engineering and product, owns launch or compute trade-offs, and reports status honestly to leadership.
Single public title. Has shipped complex products end to end in ambiguous settings, prototypes in code or with AI tools, and defines new interaction patterns for AI capabilities.

persona.tone: Warm, thoughtful and candid; low ego and genuinely curious
persona.pace: Unhurried; leaves space for the candidate to reason aloud and admit uncertainty
persona.pushback_style: Probes the reasoning behind views with 'why do you believe that?' and 'what would change your mind?', and asks for the simplest thing that would work
persona.closing_style: Invites honest questions, including critical ones about Anthropic's mission and approach

case_style.notes: PM and design cases are AI-specific (new users, trust in model limits, launch criteria) and often turn on helpfulness versus harm. TPM scenarios are system-level (capacity, release gates, slipping programs). Estimation appears mainly in capacity planning.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: principle names and descriptions follow the Anthropic careers page; principle weights are our estimate of interview emphasis, not published by Anthropic.

loop_structure: official pages confirm live coding in Colab or CodeSignal, conversational non-technical interviews, AI-free take-homes and live rounds unless stated, and the Fellows process; round order and durations come from candidate reports and prep guides. The TPM loop rests on one prep site and the design loop on one vendor guide; no reliable public source describes a loop for an 'other' family.

bar_by_level: Anthropic does not publish a ladder; level names and scope come from official job-posting titles (Senior, Staff+, Senior Staff) and their stated experience and responsibilities. Internal T-levels from anonymous posts are no longer used. PM, TPM and design show a single public title, so they are mapped to senior; there is no new-grad hire track, and the Fellows entry is a fixed-term program, not a level.

scoring_weights: derived from what Anthropic says interviews assess (experience and motivation, how candidates think through problems in real time, clarity and judgment, debugging judgment in take-homes) and from traits repeated across job postings; the numbers are our estimate.

case_style: PM cases come mainly from one prep guide plus official PM postings, TPM scenarios from one prep site, and design exercises from one vendor guide; the product versus system split is our estimate.
values_share: set to 0.35 because several reports say the culture interview is the most common rejection point and failing it ends the loop early; this is a judgment call.

sample_questions: igotanoffer.com blocked the fetcher (HTTP 403) on 2026-10-28, so its PM questions were not re-checked; TPM, research and design questions come from prep sites that aggregate candidate reports.
